facts.text: Star Ariana Madix (Catalina) later became a Bravo star on Vanderpump Rules, then hosted Peacock's Love Island USA and earned an Emmy nomination for it.
Before Ariana Madix was cast as Catalina, Dread Central's June 2011 casting report named Carlee Baker in the role, describing Catalina as a brunette lesbian bombshell.
Director Charles Band's Full Moon splashed this sequel onto shelves with a $500,000 budget, per TMDB, to a monster that began life as a cheap 1999 video-store creature feature.
Speedy turnaround: Full Moon announced the sequel in June 2011 with shooting set for the next week, showed a trailer in August, and targeted an October 2011 video release.
Jenna actress Erica Rhodes trained as a ballerina and is a classically trained cellist. Her mother is a violinist with the Boston Pops.
The script is credited to August White and Kent Roudebush, from a story by director Charles Band himself.
The original The Killer Eye (1999) was directed by David DeCoteau, who used the pseudonym Richard Chasen. Charles Band only produced it, then directed this sequel himself.
The original 1999 Killer Eye was shot in just four twelve-hour days, according to the Schlockpit's look back at director David DeCoteau's film.
Look around the mansion: props from other low-budget horror movies, like a Killjoy mask and Pinhead 3D wall art, are scattered through the house.
The 1999 Killer Eye script was first written by Neal Marshall Stevens as 'Benjamin Carr'. Director David DeCoteau disliked it, so Rolfe Kanefsky rewrote it, and it was then scaled back again.
Olivia Alexander (Giselle) once waitressed at a Los Angeles Hooters alongside future Glee star Naya Rivera and actress Raye Richards.
The 1999 Killer Eye poster art copies the old Wizard Video VHS cover of Kent Bateman's 1971 horror film The Headless Eyes.
The film is a meta-sequel: the girls watch the 1999 Killer Eye on video. Dread Central's Foywonder said scenes from that movie are replayed, leaving only about 45 minutes of new footage.
Full Moon announced this film alongside Unlucky Charms and The Dead Want Women, planning to share a small crew and locations among all three to save time and money.
Dread Central's reviewer guessed the Killer Eye movie the girls watch comes from a box for a Killer Eye prop, likely from Full Moon's FullMoonDirect.com warehouse. Merch becomes plot.
Dread Central's Foywonder gave the film 1 out of 5, calling it a "witless, frightless, pointless meta-sequel" and saying it should have ended with a cut to the Full Moon logo.
Richard Scheib of Moria gave the original Killer Eye one star, calling it 'a cheesy, cod-bad film pitched as easy sexploitation sell', though he allowed the eyeball effect was competently done.
Director Charles Band's Paramount deal for Full Moon collapsed over the budget of Lurking Fear (1994). He claimed about $300,000, but the real figure was reportedly well below $100,000.
Though shot in Los Angeles, most of the cast of the 1999 original Killer Eye affect Aussie accents, according to Richard Scheib's review at Moria.
Some IMDb contributors see the Eye's mouth-borne attack on a woman in bed as a nod to the 1984 Italian horror film Rats: Night of Terror, where a rat emerges from a victim's mouth.
The 1999 Killer Eye monster was designed by Mark Williams. The Schlockpit describes the creature as stiff, vascular and goofy.
Wikipedia's film summary notes the movie is unrated, but contains strong language, sexual content, nudity, violence and some gore.
Britain's BBFC lists this film's content warnings as strong sex, nudity, horror, gore, violence, language and sexual violence.
The original Killer Eye came out on VHS in both R-rated and unrated cuts in 1999, but didn't reach DVD until December 2003.
Around 2002 director Charles Band renamed his company Full Moon Pictures to Shadow Entertainment, feeling recent films lacked the early-'90s "Full Moon magic". The Full Moon brand later returned.
The Eye outlived the movie: it turns up in Full Moon Comix' 2018 crossover Dollman Kills the Full Moon Universe, issue 5, alongside Dollman's Brick Bardo.
Steve Miller's 2010 book 150 Movies You Should Die Before You See panned the original Killer Eye: "Nothing works in this picture." The sequel's heroine Jenna got a second chance at it.
Rotten Tomatoes lists only one critic review for this film: Felix Vasquez Jr. of Cinema Crazed, who said it is at least worth a look.
